      111 +### The logit alternative, and where it comes from            
      112  
      105 -So **the scaled score is linear in ability $\theta$, not in ra
          -w marks.** The                                                
      106 -S-shape of the tables, when plotted against % of marks, comes 
          -from the link                                                 
      107 -between raw marks and ability.                                
      113 +The more faithful alternative follows STA's documented method.
          + The                                                          
      114 +[National curriculum test handbook](https://dera.ioe.ac.uk//35
          +121/1/2019_national_curriculum_test_handbook.pdf)             
      115 +(section 13) says KS2 scaled scores are a **linear transformat
          +ion of IRT                                                    
      116 +ability** (their Equation 1, rounded down):                   
      117  
      109 -### 2. Ability is roughly the log-odds of % correct           
      110 -                                                              
      111 -In a two-parameter IRT model, the chance that a pupil of abili
          -ty $\theta$                                                   
      112 -answers question $i$ correctly is                             
      113 -                                                              
      118  ```math
      115 -P_i(\theta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-a_i(\theta - b_i)}}            
      119 +SC_i = 100 + \frac{\sigma(SC)}{\sigma(\theta)}\,\big(\theta_{X
          +_i} - \theta_{cut}\big)                                       
      120  ```
      121  
      118 -where $b_i$ is the question's difficulty and $a_i$ its discrim
          -ination. If the                                               
      119 -questions on a test are similar ($a_i \approx a$, $b_i \approx
          - b$), a pupil's                                               
      120 -proportion correct $p$ follows the same curve, and inverting i
          -t gives                                                       
      122 +In a two-parameter IRT model, the chance of a correct answer i
          +s                                                             
      123 +$P(\theta) = 1 / (1 + e^{-a(\theta - b)})$. On a test of simil
          +ar questions,                                                 
      124 +inverting it gives ability as a straight line in the log-odds 
          +of the                                                        
      125 +proportion correct, $\theta \approx b + \operatorname{logit}(p
          +)/a$ with                                                     
      126 +$\operatorname{logit}(p) = \ln\frac{p}{1-p}$. With varied ques
          +tion                                                          
      127 +difficulties the same form holds with a wider slope (the "PROX
          +" approximation;                                              
      128 +Wright and Stone, *Best Test Design*, 1979). Substituting give
          +s                                                             
      129  
      130  ```math
      123 -\theta \approx b + \frac{1}{a}\,\operatorname{logit}(p)       
      124 -```                                                           
      125 -                                                              
      126 -When question difficulties vary, the standard normal approxima
          -tion (the                                                     
      127 -"PROX" estimate; Wright and Stone, *Best Test Design*, 1979) k
          -eeps the same                                                 
      128 -form with a wider slope:                                      
      129 -                                                              
      130 -```math                                                       
      131 -\theta \approx \bar{b} + \sqrt{1 + \frac{\sigma_b^2}{2.89}}\;\
          -operatorname{logit}(p)                                        
      132 -```                                                           
      133 -                                                              
      134 -Either way, **ability is a straight line in $\operatorname{log
          -it}(p)$.**                                                    
      135 -                                                              
      136 -### 3. Substitute into STA's equation                         
      137 -                                                              
      138 -Putting step 2 into step 1, every constant collapses into two:
      139 -                                                              
      140 -```math                                                       
      131  SC \approx 100 + k\,\big(\operatorname{logit}(p) - \operatorna
           me{logit}(p_{cut})\big)

      133  
      144 -- $k$ (scaled points per logit) absorbs STA's $\sigma(SC)/\sig
          -ma(\theta)$ and                                               
      145 -  the test's item discrimination and spread.                  
      146 -- $p_{cut}$ is the proportion correct at the expected standard
      147 -  ($\theta_{cut}$).                                           
      134 +with $k = 7.3$ and $p_{cut} = 0.5$ fitted to the nine tables. 
          +Fitted per table

          +ows the S-shape                                               
      136 +of the tables comes from the raw-mark-to-ability relationship.
          + We chose the

      151 -                                                              
      152 -### 4. Fitting the constants

      154 -Grid search for the $(k, p_{cut})$ that minimises the mean abs
          -olute error

      156 -

      158 -|---|---|---|---|---|

          -44 | 1-3 |

      161 -                                                              
      162 -- Fitted per table, the formula reproduces the official tables
          - almost                                                       
      163 -  exactly. That confirms the derivation describes how the real
          - curves behave.

          -bout 8). That's

❯ are the silver tables and their purpose recorded in the first ADR?            

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Yes. ADR 0001 (already on main) covers each silver table and why it exists, in
  its "Lineage" section:
  - silver__sittings keeps every sitting, with is_scorable and an
    exclusion_reason (incomplete, deleted, survey, adaptive, year_group_above_6,
    no_responses). Sittings of deleted pupils are dropped here, which is how
    erasure flows downstream.
  - silver__answers has one answer per (sitting, question). Duplicates are
    collapsed, counting as correct only if every copy is correct, and responses
    without a sitting are dropped.
  - silver__sitting_scores holds p = correct / questions and the scaled score
    from the macro, with a link to ADR 0002 for the formula.

  There's also a lineage diagram, and the "Scale" section covers how
  silver__answers and silver__sitting_scores will be partitioned and made
  incremental in task 7.

  Comparing it with the models as built, a few small things are out of date:
  1. Grain of silver__sitting_scores: the ADR says one row per scorable sitting,
     but the model is one row per (sitting, subject), so that a sitting
     covering two subjects wouldn't break it. Today every sitting has exactly
     one subject, so the row counts are the same.
  2. The gold name is still gold__<name tbd> in the diagram. It should be
     gold__pupil_subject_scores.
  3. Columns the gold table has that the ADR doesn't list:
     meets_expected_standard, plus assessment_id and year_group_at_sitting. The
     model also names p as proportion_correct.
  4. Leftover wording from the logit version: "Why this formula and these 
     constants", although there's only one constant now (the 5% minimum).

  I can fix these: items 1 and 4 in the 07-silver-models PR, and items 2 and 3
  in 08-gold-and-reconciliation, so each PR keeps the ADR in step with what it
  adds. Shall I?

● Our line now has its own entry in the key, and it's committed on
  08-gold-and-reconciliation (444436d). The full check suite passes.

  The problem was that our line and the Atom dots were drawn in fixed colours
  outside the colour scale, so they never got a legend entry. All three layers
  now share one colour key:
  - Our formula: floor(80 + 40p) in black, drawn thicker and fully opaque.
  - Atom sittings (gold) in red.
  - The nine KS2 tables, one colour family per subject (GPS blue, maths orange,
    reading green), darker for later years. The notebook text above the chart
    says the same.

  I rendered the chart to an image to check that the key shows all of these. The
  picture also matches the numbers. Our line runs through the middle of the KS2
  bundle. It sits above the orange maths curves from about 60% upwards, which
  is where linear is generous for maths, and slightly below the reading curves
  in the middle.

  If you've already pushed 08, a plain git push adds this commit, because it's
  on top of what was there.

  The ADR 0001 touch-ups from my last message are still waiting for your
  go-ahead: the silver__sitting_scores grain, the gold model's name, the extra
  gold columns and the "constants" wording.

● That's task 7. As agreed, I'll grill you before building anything. Here are
  the facts that shape the decisions:
  - Raw tables have no updated-at timestamps. Incremental runs can only pick up
    new rows through a lookback window, not detect changes to old rows.
  - responses (100m+ rows) is the only big table. Sittings are about 1/25 of
    that, and gold is one row per scored sitting.
  - dbt 1.12 on BigQuery supports microbatch, insert_overwrite and merge
    incremental strategies, and enforced model contracts (column names and types
    checked at build time; not_null enforced; primary keys recorded but not
    enforced by BigQuery).
  - Today, silver models are views and gold is a full table.

  Task 7: making the models robust, round 1

  ❓ Q1 - Branch: 09-robust-models, stacked on 08-gold-and-reconciliation, so it
  can be raised before #10 merges.

  ➡️ Yes.

  ---

  ❓ Q2 - What to materialise how: Only make the expensive part incremental, and
  rebuild everything small in full, so that deletes and flag changes never go
  stale.

  Model: silver__answers
  Rows at scale: ~100m
  Materialisation: incremental
  Why: the only expensive scan
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Model: silver__sitting_scores
  Rows at scale: ~4m
  Materialisation: incremental, merge on (session_id, subject_id)
  Why: re-aggregates only sittings with new answers
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Model: silver__sittings
  Rows at scale: ~4m
  Materialisation: table, full rebuild each run
  Why: small, and its flags (is_deleted, is_complete) can change on any row
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Model: gold__pupil_subject_scores
  Rows at scale: ~4m
  Materialisation: table, full rebuild each run
  Why: the type-2 history is derived, so a full rebuild handles deletes and
  keeps
  valid_to correct, and it's cheap

  To make this work, the incremental models stop filtering on sitting and pupil 
  flags. Gold applies is_scorable and the deleted-pupil rule when it rebuilds,
  so a sitting deleted next month disappears from gold on the next run without
  touching the big tables.

  ➡️ Yes.

  ---

  ❓ Q3 - Incremental mechanism for silver__answers:
  - (a) microbatch, with event_time = answered_at, daily batches and lookback = 
    3. This is dbt's built-in approach for time-based data. It replaces whole
    days, so re-running a day is idempotent, and backfills run with
    --event-time-start/--event-time-end.
  - (b) insert_overwrite on date(answered_at) partitions with a hand-written
    lookback filter. Similar, but more manual.
  - (c) merge on (session_id, question_id). This scans the key on every run,
    which is the costliest at 100m rows.

  All duplicate copies of an answer share an answered_at, so they always land in
  the same batch and the de-duplication stays correct.

  ➡️ (a) microbatch, with the table partitioned by date(answered_at) and
  clustered by session_id.

  ---

  ❓ Q4 - Changes outside the lookback window: Without updated-at timestamps, a
  response changed more than 3 days later won't be picked up by an incremental
  run. Options:
  - Document a scheduled --full-refresh (for example weekly) as the backstop.
  - Make the lookback (answers_lookback_days, default 3) a var.

  Deletes and flag changes are unaffected, because gold rebuilds in full (Q2).

  ➡️ Yes to both. The README and ADR 0001 say this plainly.

  ---

  ❓ Q5 - Contracts: Enforced contracts on all four models:
  - every column listed, with data_type and a description
  - not_null constraints on the keys
  - a primary_key constraint, which BigQuery records but doesn't enforce
  - on_schema_change: fail for the incremental models, so a schema change can't
    slip in silently

  ➡️ Yes.

  ---

  ❓ Q6 - Drop the no_responses exclusion reason? Working it out means counting
  responses (100m rows) inside silver__sittings on every full rebuild. A sitting
  with no responses just gets no score row, which is the same outcome.

  ➡️ Yes. Remove it from silver__sittings, and update the ADR's list of
  exclusion reasons.

  ---

  ❓ Q7 - Proving it's idempotent and incremental-safe: Add a small dbt macro,
  table_fingerprint (row count plus an order-independent content hash), and a
  make verify target that:
  1. builds twice and checks nothing changed (idempotent)
  2. compares an incremental build with a --full-refresh build (incremental
     equals full)

  ➡️ Yes. It's a repeatable check that doesn't make the reconciliation notebook
  bigger.

  ---

  ❓ Q8 - dbt tests: AGENTS.md says to agree test behaviour with you first. I
  propose:
  - unique + not_null on each model's key, using
    dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns for composite keys
  - scaled_score between 80 and 120 when has_scaled_score
  - exactly one is_current row per (pupil, subject)
  - gold's valid_to equal to the next row's valid_from

  All at severity: error.

  ➡️ Yes to all four. Or tell me which behaviours you'd rather enforce.

● Answers to your two questions, then one more round.

  Q6: "every full rebuild" means every dbt build, not just --full-refresh.
  silver__sittings is a plain table, and dbt rebuilds a plain table from scratch
  on every run. Only incremental models get the "process only new data"
  treatment. So the no_responses reason would make every normal run count all
  100m+ responses, which defeats the point of making silver__answers
  incremental. Dropping it keeps the ordinary run cheap.

  Q7: yes, there's a smaller-scale option: dbt unit tests (built into dbt since
  1.8). You write a few input rows and the expected output in YAML, and dbt
  checks the model's logic against those rows alone. It takes milliseconds,
  costs almost nothing in BigQuery, runs inside the normal dbt build, and so is
  covered by the pre-push hook on every change. A unit test can also pretend a 
  run is incremental: it supplies made-up "already loaded" rows for the existing
  table, so the incremental path is tested directly.

  That covers what matters for being robust (the de-duplication rule, the
  formula's edge cases, and the type-2 history logic) without a full double
  build. I'd drop the make verify idea and use unit tests instead. Idempotency
  then rests on determinism by construction (no random IDs, no
  current_timestamp(), full ordering in window functions), which the unit tests
  check rule by rule.

  Settled so far: microbatch for answers (Q3), a full refresh documented as the
  backstop for late changes (Q4), contracts noted in the README as a future
  improvement (Q5), and the four tests from Q8. You didn't answer Q1 (stack on
  08) or Q2 (materialisations); they're repeated below.

  ❓ Q9 - Which behaviours the unit tests pin down (AGENTS.md says to agree
  these first):

  Model: silver__answers
  Behaviour enforced: Duplicate copies collapse to one row, correct only if
  every
  copy is correct. In incremental mode, re-processing an already-loaded day
  produces the same row, not a second one.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Model: silver__sitting_scores
  Behaviour enforced: Formula edge cases: 0 out of 20 → no score; 1 out of 20
  (exactly 5%) → 82; 1 out of 21 (below 5%) → no score; 50% → 100; 100% → 120;
  and rounding down (e.g. 2 out of 3 → 106).
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Model: gold__pupil_subject_scores
  Behaviour enforced: Two sittings for one pupil and subject → valid_to of the
  first = valid_from of the second, and only the second is current. Unscorable
  sittings and deleted pupils are left out. A subject with no score row
  (has_scaled_score false) is still a history row.

  They live in YAML under unit_tests: next to each model.

  ➡️ Yes, these behaviours. Or add or remove any.

● Building it now on 09-robust-models. One thing I'll flag as I go: with
  microbatch, the "already-loaded day isn't duplicated" guarantee comes from dbt
  replacing whole days, not from the model's SQL. A unit test only checks the
  SQL, so it can't show that. I'll put the incremental-mode unit test on
  silver__sitting_scores instead, whose own SQL does the incremental work.

       1 +-- Within a (pupil, subject), each row's valid_to is the next r
         +ow's                                                           
       2 +-- valid_from, so the history has no gaps or overlaps.

  Notes: Partitioned by day and clustered by session_id. Re-running a day

  Model: silver__sitting_scores

  Notes: Re-scores every sitting that has an answer in the lookback, using all

  Model: silver__sittings

  Model: gold__pupil_subject_scores
  Build: table, rebuilt every run
  Notes: Now applies the scorable-sitting and deleted-pupil rules itself, so

  Two findings, now in the README and ADR 0001:
  1. The raw responses table isn't partitioned. Each daily batch reads 8.9 MiB,
     the whole table, so at 100m rows every batch would do a full scan. Atom
     would need to partition de_raw.responses by date(answered_at) upstream for
     the batches to read only their own day. That's now the first item under
     "What I would do next".
  2. Unit tests on incremental models check their fixtures against the live 
     table's columns. The fixture for the existing table failed while BigQuery
     still had the old view. I rewrote that fixture as SQL so it works whatever
     is in the warehouse.

  Two changes from what we agreed:
  - The "re-processing a day isn't duplicated" guarantee for silver__answers
    comes from dbt's microbatch, which replaces whole days, so a unit test can't
    show it. I unit-tested the incremental behaviour on silver__sitting_scores
    instead, and checked run-twice and incremental-vs-full-refresh against
    BigQuery.
  - While I was editing ADR 0001, I also made the earlier small fixes: the gold
    model's name, the (sitting, subject) grain, the extra gold columns and the
    exclusion-reason list.

● Both additions are committed on 09-robust-models (3531c38), and the full check
  suite passes.

  The new notebook section ("5. Distribution of the final scores") has:
  - A per-subject table: sittings, mean, standard deviation,
    5th/25th/50th/75th/95th percentiles, the share of scores in 95–109, the
    share meeting the expected standard, and the share at exactly 80 or 120.
  - Two histograms: every scored sitting, and each pupil's current score per
    subject, each with its own y-axis so the smaller one isn't squashed.
  - A findings note. Scores bunch in the middle and the ends of the scale are
    barely used:

  ┌────────────────┬───────┬─────┬──────────┬─────────────┬─────────────────┐
  │                │ Mean  │ SD  │ Middle   │  Share in   │    5th–95th     │
  │                │       │     │   half   │   95–109    │   percentile    │
  ├────────────────┼───────┼─────┼──────────┼─────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ All scored     │ 102.2 │ 7.9 │ 96–108   │ 64%         │ 88–115          │
  │ sittings       │       │     │          │             │                 │
  ├────────────────┼───────┼─────┼──────────┼─────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ English        │ 102.3 │ 7.6 │ 97–108   │ 67%         │ 90–114          │
  ├────────────────┼───────┼─────┼──────────┼─────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ Maths          │ 102.3 │ 7.9 │ 97–108   │ 63%         │ 88–116          │
  └────────────────┴───────┴─────┴──────────┴─────────────┴─────────────────┘

  The note also explains the comb-like spikes in the histogram: most sittings
  share a few lengths, so some integer scores come up more often than others.

  The README now has this item under "What I would do next": find a curve that
  spreads scores out more. It lists two options:
  - A steeper curve through the middle. The logit from ADR 0002 would make
    things worse: it's flatter in the middle (40–60% maps to 97–102, against
    96–104 for linear).
  - Calibrating to the national KS2 distribution. Map each pupil's percentile
    among Atom pupils in the same year group to the national scaled score at
    that percentile. I haven't checked whether DfE publishes a full national
    score distribution in a form we could use, so check that before relying on
    this option.

  Either would ship as a new scoring_method.

  has its two unpushed commits; 09 sits on top of it.

       97 +## Robust table design                                        
       98 +                                                              
       99 +How the models meet the brief's "built to last" requirements. 
          +Details are in                                                
      100 +[ADR 0001](docs/adr/0001-scoring-data-model.md).              
      101 +                                                              
      102 +**Done**                                                      
      103 +                                                              
      104 +- **Re-runnable:** keys are hashes of natural keys (no random 
          +IDs or                                                        
      105 +  timestamps), daily batches and sittings are replaced whole, 
          +and small tables                                              
      106 +  are rebuilt every run. Checked: running twice gives identica
          +l tables, and an                                              
      107 +  incremental build gives the same tables as a full refresh.  
      108 +- **Incremental for 100m+ responses:** `silver__answers` is bu
          +ilt in daily                                                  
      109 +  batches (dbt microbatch, 3-day lookback, partitioned by day,
          + clustered by                                                 
      110 +  sitting); `silver__sitting_scores` merges only sittings with
          + new answers.                                                 
      111 +  A normal run reprocesses 4 days.                            
      112 +- **Point in time:** gold is a type-2 history (`valid_from` / 
          +`valid_to` /                                                  
      113 +  `is_current`), so any pupil's score can be recomputed as it 
          +stood at time T.                                              
      114 +- **Deletes and corrections flow through:** sitting and pupil 
          +rules are                                                     
      115 +  applied in gold, which is rebuilt every run, so a deleted si
          +tting or pupil                                                
      116 +  disappears on the next run.                                 
      117 +- **Tested and documented:** every column has a description; d
          +ata tests                                                     
      118 +  (unique keys, 80-120 range, one current row, unbroken histor
          +y) and unit                                                   
      119 +  tests (de-duplication, formula edge cases, incremental logic
          +, history) run                                                
      120 +  in every `dbt build`, including the pre-push hook.          
      121 +                                                              
      122 +**Would do next**                                             
      123 +                                                              
      124 +- **Model contracts:** enforce column names, data types and `n
          +ot_null` /                                                    
      125 +  primary-key constraints, so a schema change fails the build 
          +instead of                                                    
      126 +  reaching the application database.                          
      127 +- **Partition `de_raw.responses` by `date(answered_at)`** upst
          +ream, so each                                                 
      128 +  daily batch reads only its own day.                         
      129 +- **Schedule the weekly `--full-refresh`** (and normal runs) i
          +n an                                                          
      130 +  orchestrator, as the backstop for late changes.             
      131 +- **Run `dbt build` in CI** against a dev dataset (needs workl
          +oad identity                                                  
      132 +  federation for BigQuery access).                            
      133 +- **Export to the application database:** version the gold mod
          +el and sync it                                                
      134 +  incrementally, using the surrogate key and `valid_from`.    
      135 +                                                              
      136  ## How the pieces fit together
      137  
      138  ```

     (at most 5), roughly the same as the official tables differ from year to
     year. It agrees on "met the expected standard" for 94–100% of raw scores,

     the middle (mean 102, middle half 96–108, about two thirds in 95–109), so a
     curve with a more even spread would help. It links to the matching "What I
     would do next" item and explains the comb-like pattern.

❯ add a section to the readme to indicate that the prerquisites to running this 
  repo is to have uv installed (I don't think another tool like peotry is       
  compatible with this pyproject.toml is it?)                                   

● Short answer: in practice, no. The pyproject.toml relies on three uv-specific
  things:
  - uv.lock: the pinned versions are only read by uv.
  - [tool.uv] override-dependencies: this is what stops
    dbt-core-experimental-parser from being installed. With pip or Poetry, that
    package would be built again and you'd hit the same
    CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED error as before.
  - [dependency-groups]: this is the newer PEP 735 format for dev dependencies,
    which pip and Poetry don't install the way uv does. I'm not certain about
    Poetry's support in its latest versions, so I'll keep the README wording
    general.

  There's also no [build-system] table, so pip install . would try to package
  the repo itself.

  I'll add a "Prerequisites" section above "Quick start".

● I've added a "Prerequisites" section to the README, just above "Quick start".
  It's committed on 09-robust-models (ad50656), and the full check suite passes.

  On your question: I wouldn't rely on Poetry or pip working with this
  pyproject.toml:
  - uv.lock holds the pinned versions, and only uv reads it.
  - [tool.uv] override-dependencies is what keeps dbt-core-experimental-parser
    out of the install. Without it, pip or Poetry would try to build that
    package and could hit the same CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED error you saw
    earlier.
  - [dependency-groups] is a newer format (PEP 735) for the dev tools, such as
    marimo, ruff and sqruff, which pip and Poetry don't handle the way uv does.
    I'm not sure whether recent Poetry versions support it.
  - There's no [build-system] table, so pip install . would try to package the
    repo itself.

  The section lists:
  - uv: it also installs Python 3.12 itself, so no separate Python install is
    needed. The section says pip and Poetry aren't supported, and why.
  - gcloud CLI: logged in, with access to the atom-analytics-candidates BigQuery
    project.
  - make and git.

● Yes. The Python version is pinned in two places, both committed since the
  first PR:
  - .python-version contains 3.12. uv reads it to decide which Python to install
    and use for .venv, and downloads it if it isn't already on the machine.
  - pyproject.toml has requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.13". uv refuses to resolve
    or install with any other Python version, so the two can't drift apart.

  That's why the new Prerequisites section can say uv installs the right Python
  itself.

● Here's what the research says before we decide anything.

  How well KS2 predicts GCSE: "neither a terrible nor an excellent predictor".
  - Cambridge Assessment (Benton & Sutch, 2013)
    (https://www.cambridgeassessment.org.uk/Images/181034-exploring-the-value-of
    -gcse-prediction-matrices-based-upon-attainment-at-key-stage-2.pdf) found
    the correlation between KS2 and a pupil's grade in a GCSE subject is about
    0.5 on average (the median across subjects). That compares with over 0.6 for
    KS3 and about 0.7 for the pupil's other GCSEs. Very few subjects exceed 0.7
    with KS2, and about 1 in 10 are below 0.4.
  - Ofqual (2014)
    (https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a82f24140f0b62305b952a8/201
    4-06-16-analysis-of-use-of-key-stage-2-data-in-gcse-predictions.pdf) found
    the same correlation of about 0.5 across several ways of measuring KS2. KS2
    category explained about 38% of the variation in GCSE grade.
  - In plain terms, a correlation of 0.5 means KS2 explains roughly a quarter to
    a third of the differences between pupils. That supports your instinct:
    it's good for grouping pupils, weak for an individual pupil's grade.

  How others do it:
  - DfE publishes transition matrices and Progress 8 estimates
    (https://gov.uk/government/publications/ready-reckoners-and-transition-matri
    ces-for-key-stage-4): the national spread of GCSE grades for all pupils with
    the same prior attainment, measured as the average of the KS2 reading and
    maths scaled scores.
  - FFT Aspire (https://ffteducationdatalab.org.uk/2022/11/a-quick-overview-of-f
    ft-estimates-for-secondary-schools/) fits a multinomial logistic regression
    on prior attainment, gender, month of birth and subject, and reports a
    spread of likely grades, not a single grade. Its contextual version also
    adds disadvantage and school factors. FFT notes that health, attendance,
    school moves and motivation all move outcomes, and none of them are in the
    model.
  - Known caveats (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.06299): KS2 scores contain
    measurement error, the bottom of the scale is cut off, and the national KS2
    baseline is under threat (FFT, 2025 (https://ffteducationdatalab.org.uk/2025
    /11/contextualising-attainment-without-key-stage-2-baselines/)).

  Part 3: GCSE prediction, round 1

  ❓ Q1 - Form of the answer: The brief says "a few paragraphs is a complete
  answer". Should it go in a new README section, "Predicting GCSE results", of
  about 4–6 short paragraphs or bullets with sources? It would be on a new
  branch, 10-gcse-prediction, from main.

  ➡️ Yes, in the README, so the reviewer reads it in the same place as
  everything else. No separate document.

  ---

  ❓ Q2 - What we predict: Should we predict a spread of likely grades (9–1) per
  GCSE subject, reported as the most likely grade plus a range ("most likely a
  6; 70% chance of 5–7")? That's what FFT does. The alternative is a single
  grade or a single Attainment 8 score.

  ➡️ A spread per subject. With a correlation of about 0.5, a single grade would
  claim more certainty than the data supports.

  ---

  ❓ Q3 - The data needed:
  1. GCSE outcomes linked to the same pupils. This is the blocker: Atom doesn't
     have them. They could come from partner schools sharing results, or from
     DfE's National Pupil Database (NPD) through an approved data-sharing route.
  2. Prior attainment: official KS2 results where available, plus Atom's own 
     history: scaled scores over time (the trend matters as well as the level),
     topic-level strengths, consistency and engagement.
  3. Context: month of birth, gender, disadvantage (free school meals / pupil
     premium), special educational needs (SEN), English as an additional
     language (EAL), attendance and the secondary school attended.

  ➡️ All three, with item 1 flagged as the main dependency and the hardest to
  get.

  ---

  ❓ Q4 - How to use sensitive context (disadvantage, SEN, ethnicity): Building
  it into each pupil's prediction makes it more accurate. But it can lower
  expectations for exactly the pupils who most need support, which is the
  criticism of contextual targets. Options:
  - (a) Prediction uses prior attainment, Atom history, month of birth and
    school. Sensitive context is used only to check fairness (is the model as
    accurate for disadvantaged pupils?) and for school-level reporting.
  - (b) Build everything into the prediction.

  ➡️ (a). Say why in one sentence.

  ---

  ❓ Q5 - Modelling approach: Keep it simple, since the brief isn't testing
  statistics:
  - Baseline: DfE-style transition matrices (grade spread by prior-attainment
    band).
  - Then: an ordered logistic regression per GCSE subject, adding Atom's
    features.
  - Evaluate on later cohorts the model hasn't seen: % of pupils within one
    grade, whether the stated probabilities are honest (calibration), and
    comparison with the baseline.

  ➡️ Yes. More complex models only if they clearly beat this.

  ---

  ❓ Q6 - Assumptions to state:
  - Our KS2-style scores are comparable to real KS2 results. That's ADR 0002's
    assumption, and it's the weakest link.
  - The relationships hold across five years and across cohorts, despite
    curriculum and grade-boundary changes and the disrupted 2020–21 grading.
  - Atom users are like the population the model will be used on. They may skew
    towards engaged or 11+ families.
  - Pupils whose GCSE results we can't get are missing at random.

  ➡️ Yes, those four, each with a line on why it matters.

  ---

  ❓ Q7 - Mapping Atom subjects to GCSEs:
  - Maths → GCSE Maths
  - English → GCSE English Language and Literature
  - Science → Combined Science, if Science sittings ever exist
  - Verbal and Non-Verbal Reasoning → general ability features feeding into
    every subject

  ➡️ Yes, one sentence in the write-up.

  "most likely 6, probably 5–7"), never a single grade.

  What the section will say: (1) GCSE results linked to the same pupils. Atom

  primary-school work.

● The part 3 section is written, but not committed yet. dbt build failed because
  the GCP token has expired again, not because of the change: it's README-only
  and every static check passed. The change is staged on 10-gcse-prediction,
  branched from the latest main, which includes PR #11. Refresh the token with:

  gcloud auth print-access-token > .gcp_token

  Then I'll re-run the checks and commit.

  The new section, "Predicting GCSE results from primary-school work", sits
  after "Robust table design", so the README follows the brief's three parts in
  order. It's in plain English:
  - Start with the purpose: who uses the prediction, and how much they'll rely
    on it.
  - Predict a spread, not a single grade. This is justified by accuracy:
    - KS2 correlates about 0.5 with a pupil's grade in a GCSE subject,
      explaining roughly a quarter to a third of the differences between pupils
      (Cambridge Assessment: very few subjects above 0.7; Ofqual: about 38% of
      the variation).
    - That's useful for groups, weak for one pupil.
    - FFT reports spreads for the same reason.
  - Data: two essentials (GCSE results linked to the same pupils, the main
    dependency; and primary-school work, meaning KS2 plus Atom's history). Then
    a "nice to have" bullet that also carries the sensitive-data point, as you
    asked: it could lower expectations, so it's used only to check the model is
    equally accurate for every group.
  - Model: logistic regression per subject against DfE's transition matrices,
    tested on later years of pupils: within one grade, and whether the stated
    chances hold up.
  - Subjects: the Atom-to-GCSE subject mapping.
  - Assumptions, each with why it matters.
  - Sources: links to the four documents (Cambridge Assessment, Ofqual, FFT
    Education Datalab, DfE transition matrices).

      156 +                                                              
      157 +### Assumptions                                               
      158 +                                                              
      159 +Scoring follows the KS2 rules in the GOV.UK guidance where the
          +y apply.                                                      
      160 +                                                              
      161 +- **Conversion to the 80-120 scale:** linear rescaling for eve
          +ry subject,                                                   
      162 +  `floor(80 + 40p)` (0% → 80, 50% → 100, 100% → 120); no score
          + (`N`) below 5%,                                              
      163 +  never rounded up to 80. The official tables aren't applied d
          +irectly because                                               
      164 +  an Atom assessment isn't the KS2 paper they were calibrated 
          +on                                                            
      165 +  ([ADR 0002](docs/adr/0002-scaled-score-curve.md)).          
      166 +- **An Atom assessment is about as hard as a KS2 paper**, and 
          +one question is                                               
      167 +  worth one mark.                                             
      168 +- **Subjects:** every subject with qualifying sittings is scor
          +ed (English,                                                  
      169 +  Maths, Screeners, Verbal and Non-Verbal Reasoning). Science 
          +has questions                                                 
      170 +  but no sittings; Wellbeing sittings are all surveys (no righ
          +t answers).                                                   
      171 +- **Qualifying sittings:** complete, not deleted, not a survey
          + and not an                                                   
      172 +  adaptive mock (adaptive difficulty makes % correct incompara
          +ble), year group                                              
      173 +  1-6. KS2 precedent: a pupil must sit every paper to receive 
          +a score.                                                      
      174 +- **Orphan responses** are excluded: without a sitting we can'
          +t apply the rules                                             
      175 +  above.                                                      
      176 +- **Duplicates** are treated as an upstream double-submission 
          +bug: one answer                                               
      177 +  per (sitting, question), correct only if every copy is corre
          +ct. Mean %                                                    
      178 +  correct moves by under 2 points under "any copy correct" ins
          +tead.                                                         
      179 +- **No-attempts** count as wrong (0 marks), as an unanswered K
          +S2 question does.                                             
      180 +- **Late answers** are kept (they are at most 1 second late). 
      181 +- **Unit of scoring:** each qualifying sitting is scored on it
          +s own (KS2 never                                              
      182 +  pools attempts). A pupil's score as of time T is their lates
          +t scored sitting                                              
      183 +  finished at or before T.                                    
      184 +                                                              
      185 +### What I would do next                                      
      186 +

          +steeper curve

          +aled-score

          +m pupils of the                                               
      191 +  same year group to the national score at that percentile. Ei
          +ther would need                                               
      192 +  a new `scoring_method`.

      194 +  Atom responses, removing the "as hard as a KS2 paper" assump

      221 -## How the pieces fit together                                
      222 -                                                              
      223 -```                                                           
      224 -de_raw (sources, bronze) ─┬─ silver__sittings        every sit
          -ting + is_scorable / exclusion_reason                         
      225 -                          ├─ silver__answers         one answe
          -r per (sitting, question), duplicates collapsed               
      226 -                          └─ silver__sitting_scores  floor(80 
          -+ 40 * correct / questions)                                   
      227 -                                       └─ gold__pupil_subject_
          -scores  type-2 history per pupil × subject                    
      228 -```                                                           
      229 -                                                              
      230 -- `macros/ks2_scaled_score.sql`: the scoring formula, in one p
          -lace; the                                                     
      231 -  minimum for a score is a dbt var in `dbt_project.yml`.      
      232 -- `seeds/ks2_scaled_score_conversion.csv`: official KS2 tables
          - (2024-2026),                                                 
      233 -  used to calibrate and check the formula, not for scoring.   
      234 -- Notebooks: `01_exploration` (data profiling), `02_conversion
          -_curves`                                                      
      235 -  (choosing the formula), `03_reconciliation` (compares our sc
          -ores with the                                                 
      236 -  official KS2 conversion tables).                            
      237 -                                                              
      238 -## Data quality issues                                        
      239 -                                                              
      240 -Evidence for each is in [`notebooks/01_exploration.py`](notebo
          -oks/01_exploration.py)                                        
      241 -(`uv run marimo edit notebooks/01_exploration.py`).           
      242 -                                                              
      243 -- **Orphan responses:** 1,433 `responses` rows (56 sessions) r
          -eference a                                                    
      244 -  `session_id` missing from `assessment_sittings`.            
      245 -- **Duplicate responses:** 2,082 `(session_id, question_id)` p
          -airs have more                                                
      246 -  than one row (4,493 rows), all in complete summative fixed-q
          -uestion sittings.                                             
      247 -  Copies share `answered_at`, `seconds_taken` and `question_nu
          -mber` but have                                                
      248 -  distinct `response_id`s, and in 965 pairs they disagree on `
          -is_correct`.                                                  
      249 -  The copy count varies by pupil for the same question, so the
          -se are not                                                    
      250 -  multi-mark questions; they sit inside one sitting, so they a
          -re not re-sits.                                               
      251 -- **`responses.session_type`** is always `MOCK_TEST` and never
          - matches the                                                  
      252 -  sitting's `session_type`.                                   
      253 -- **Late answers:** 1,608 responses have `answered_at` after t
          -he sitting's                                                  
      254 -  `finished_at`, but by at most 1 second (timestamp rounding).
          - Only                                                         
      255 -  incomplete sittings lack a `finished_at`.                   
      256 -- **Soft deletes:** no pupil or sitting is currently marked `i
          -s_deleted`.                                                   
      257 -- **Year groups:** 25 sittings (entrance exams) are in years 1
          -1, 14 and 15.                                                 
      258 -- **Unused rows:** 61 pupils have no sittings, 79 sittings hav
          -e no responses,                                               
      259 -  and 8,096 of 10,552 questions in `course_hierarchy` have nev
          -er been answered.                                             
      260 -                                                              
      261 -## Assumptions                                                
      262 -                                                              
      263 -Scoring follows the KS2 rules in the GOV.UK guidance where the
          -y apply.                                                      
      264 -                                                              
      265 -- **Conversion to the 80-120 scale:** linear rescaling for eve
          -ry subject,                                                   
      266 -  `floor(80 + 40p)`, where `p` is the proportion of questions 
          -correct (0% →                                                 
      267 -  80, 50% → 100, 100% → 120); no score (`N`) below 5%. It is w
          -ithin about 1.5                                               
      268 -  points of the official 2024-2026 KS2 tables on average (evid
          -ence in                                                       
      269 -  [`notebooks/02_conversion_curves.py`](notebooks/02_conversio
          -n_curves.py) and                                              
      270 -  [ADR 0002](docs/adr/0002-scaled-score-curve.md)). The real t
          -ables aren't                                                  
      271 -  applied directly because an Atom assessment isn't the KS2 pa
          -per they were                                                 
      272 -  calibrated on.                                              
      273 -- **Assumes** an Atom assessment is about as hard as a KS2 pap
          -er and one                                                    
      274 -  question is worth one mark. With more data, question difficu
          -lty could be                                                  
      275 -  estimated from Atom responses to adjust for this.           
      276 -- **Subjects:** every subject with qualifying sittings is scor
          -ed (English,                                                  
      277 -  Maths, Screeners, Verbal and Non-Verbal Reasoning). Science 
          -has questions                                                 
      278 -  but no sittings; Wellbeing sittings are all surveys (no righ
          -t answers).                                                   
      279 -- **Qualifying sittings:** complete, not deleted, not a survey
          - and not an                                                   
      280 -  adaptive mock (adaptive difficulty makes % correct incompara
          -ble), year group                                              
      281 -  1-6. KS2 precedent: a pupil must sit every paper to receive 
          -a score.                                                      
      282 -- **Orphan responses** are excluded: without a sitting we can'
          -t apply the rules                                             
      283 -  above.                                                      
      284 -- **Duplicates** are treated as an upstream double-submission 
          -bug: one answer                                               
      285 -  per (sitting, question), correct only if every copy is corre
          -ct. Mean %                                                    
      286 -  correct moves by under 2 points under "any copy correct" ins
          -tead.                                                         
      287 -- **No-attempts** count as wrong (0 marks), as an unanswered K
          -S2 question does.                                             
      288 -- **Late answers** are kept (they are at most 1 second late). 
      289 -- **Unit of scoring:** each qualifying sitting is scored on it
          -s own (KS2 never                                              
      290 -  pools attempts). A pupil's score as of time T is their lates
          -t scored sitting                                              
      291 -  finished at or before T.                                    
      292 -- **Below the minimum raw score** a pupil gets no scaled score
          - (`N`, outcome                                                
      293 -  `NS`), as in the GOV.UK guidance; we don't round them up to 
          -80.                                                           
      294 -                                                              
      295 -## Running it                                                 
      296 -                                                              
      297 -- `make build` runs `dbt build`: models, seeds, data tests and
          - unit tests.                                                  
      298 -  `silver__answers` and `silver__sitting_scores` are increment
          -al, so a normal                                               
      299 -  run only reprocesses the last `answers_lookback_days` (3) da
          -ys of answers.                                                
      300 -- **Schedule a full refresh** (`dbt build --full-refresh`, e.g
          -. weekly). The                                                
      301 -  raw tables have no updated-at timestamps, so a response chan
          -ged after the                                                 
      302 -  lookback window is only picked up by a full refresh. Changes
          - to sittings and                                              
      303 -  pupils (deletes, completions) are picked up by every normal 
          -run.                                                          
      304 -- To rebuild a date range of answers: `dbt build --select silv
          -er__answers+                                                  
      305 -  --event-time-start 2026-01-01 --event-time-end 2026-02-01`. 
      306 -                                                              
      307 -## What I would do next                                       
      308 -                                                              
      309 -- **A curve that spreads scores out more evenly.** Under the l
          -inear formula,                                                
      310 -  scores bunch in the middle: across all scored sittings the m
          -iddle half is                                                 
      311 -  about 96-108, and around two thirds fall in 95-109, so the e
          -nds of the 80-120                                             
      312 -  scale are barely used (see [Results](#2-the-distribution-cou
          -ld-be-more-even)).                                            
      313 -  Options: a steeper curve through the middle (the logit in AD
          -R 0002 is                                                     
      314 -  *flatter* there, so it would bunch scores further), or calib
          -rating to the                                                 
      315 -  national KS2 scaled-score distribution, i.e. mapping each pu
          -pil's                                                         
      316 -  percentile among Atom pupils of the same year group to the n
          -ational score                                                 
      317 -  at that percentile. Either would need a new `scoring_method`
          -.                                                             
      318 -                                                              
      319 -- **Partition `de_raw.responses` by `date(answered_at)`** (ups
          -tream). The daily                                             
      320 -  batches of `silver__answers` filter on it, but today each ba
          -tch still scans                                               
      321 -  the whole raw table.                                        
      322 -                                                              
      323 -- **Model contracts:** enforce the schema of each model (colum
          -n names, data                                                 
      324 -  types, `not_null` / primary-key constraints) with dbt model 
          -contracts, so a                                               
      325 -  type change fails the build instead of reaching the applicat
          -ion database.                                                 
      326 -

❯ is it possible to transfer ownership of a github repo or make it visible just 
  to a few individuals?                                                         

● Yes, both are possible.

  Transfer ownership: Settings → General → Danger Zone → Transfer ownership.
  Enter the new owner's username or organisation name and confirm.
  - The recipient has to accept the transfer, by email, before it completes.
  - Issues, PRs, stars and watchers move with the repo, and GitHub redirects the
    old URL and git remote to the new location.
  - You lose admin rights unless the new owner adds you back as a collaborator.
  - If the target is an organisation, you need permission to create repos there.

  Visible to just a few people: make the repo private (Settings → General →
  Danger Zone → Change visibility). Then invite each person under Settings →
  Collaborators → Add people.
  - Only you and the people you invite can see it.
  - Each person has to accept the invitation.
  - A personal account can invite unlimited collaborators to private repos on
    the free plan.
  - You can choose their access level: Read is enough for reviewing, Write if
    they need to push.

  For a take-home, the usual approach is the second one. Keep it private and add
  the reviewers as collaborators with Read access, using the GitHub usernames
  the recruitment team gives you, then send them the link. You keep ownership,
  and you can remove their access afterwards. Before that, check whether Atom
  asked for a public repo or a particular way of sharing; the brief only says
  "push your work to a GitHub repository and send us the link".

  The repo was public, since I could fetch it without credentials. Going private
  won't remove copies anyone has already cloned. Anything already pushed, like
  the BigQuery project name, has already been visible. As far as I know, no
  secrets were ever committed, because .gcp_token is gitignored.
